title: Bring Back Bildung
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: Andrew Cantarutti takes on the familiar claim that schools were built in Prussia to produce obedient workers and soldiers, pointing out that the loudest voices repeating it today, such as Sal Khan and Alpha School's MacKenzie Price, are selling ed-tech products. Citing Audrey Watters and Sherman Dorn, he calls the factory model critique a rhetorical foil for the sales pitch. The real architect of the Prussian system, Wilhelm von Humboldt, believed almost the opposite: that education should develop the individual as a whole person, free from the interests of the state. Humboldt's idea of Bildung rested on four premises: universal formation across classes, general education before specialization, freedom, and knowledge for its own sake. After 1848 the state reasserted control and Bildung became a credential for the middle class. Cantarutti concludes that the market is now the power that wants a predetermined product from schools, and invites readers to ask what kind of people we hope children will become.
points: The Prussian factory-school story is often a sales pitch, since the people who repeat it sell the technology that is supposed to replace the factory.
Humboldt designed the Prussian system to form free, autonomous individuals and wanted the state to measure itself against them, which is the opposite of the factory caricature.
Bildung rests on universal formation, general education before specialization, freedom and knowledge for its own sake.
Humboldt would have opposed teaching arithmetic through commerce, arguing that mixing vocation with general education produces neither complete humans nor complete citizens.
Today the pressure on schools comes less from the state than from the market, so a free people must be able to judge the companies selling to schools.
quotes: The same people who speak for a 400 billion dollar industry seem to dislike the so-called industrial model of education.
In other words, the Prussian critique is often the sales pitch for what I’ve called the Marketplace Mirror.
Importantly, the whole of this system was designed to support the formation of the individual, free from extrinsic influence, free from politics, war, and industry.
He rejected the necessity for an “intellectual aristocracy” and believed that the most ordinary labourer and the most privileged socialite must begin from the same foundation.

He argued that mixing them produced neither complete human beings nor complete citizens. His example was in teaching arithmetic: if you teach a child to count and compute using coins, mathematics becomes tied to commerce, shopping, and transactional value from the outset.
He believed that education should aim at the student as a whole person, not at the role they might fill in society.
Bildung shifted from a universal ideal to the marker of a credentialed and educated middle class. It became an instrument of selection, rather than one of freedom.
Industry looks different today, but it’s still industry. Humboldt was concerned by the state, but his logic holds for any power that wants a predetermined product from its schools.
